name: Maine

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Maine became the 23rd state on March 15, 1820.

events.title: 1830 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1830 census, Maine's House delegation grew from 7 to 8 seats.

events.title: 1840 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1840 census, Maine's House delegation shrank from 8 to 7 seats.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, Maine's House delegation shrank from 7 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, Maine's House delegation shrank from 6 to 5 seats.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Maine kept 5 seats in the House.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Maine's House delegation shrank from 5 to 4 seats.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 48th Congress (1883–1885), Maine elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Maine kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Maine kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Maine kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Maine's House delegation shrank from 4 to 3 seats.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Maine kept 3 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Maine kept 3 seats in the House.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Maine's House delegation shrank from 3 to 2 seats.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Maine kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Maine kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Maine kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Maine kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: State supreme court draws the map
events.text: When the legislature did not pass a congressional plan by the constitutional deadline, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court issued the districts itself on July 2, 2003.

events.title: Redistricting schedule moved up
events.text: In November 2011, Maine voters approved Question 4, a constitutional amendment moving redistricting from years ending in 3 to years ending in 1, starting in 2021. It also required a two-thirds vote of the legislature to adopt congressional plans.

events.title: Desena v. Maine
events.text: Maine's schedule called for redrawing districts in 2013. A three-judge federal court ruled in June 2011 that the existing districts were unequal under the 2010 census and could not be used in 2012; the legislature passed a new map that September.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Maine kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Commission plan enacted after delay
events.text: Because census data arrived late, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court extended the redistricting deadlines in July 2021. The Apportionment Commission approved a congressional map on September 24, and the legislature enacted it on September 29, 2021.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Maine kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c018.text: New map drawn after the 1820 census. It was first used in the 1822 election.

c023.text: New map drawn after the 1830 census, which raised Maine's seats from 7 to 8. It was first used in the 1832 election.

c028.text: New map drawn after the 1840 census, which cut Maine's seats from 8 to 7. It was first used in the 1842 election.

c029.text: Maine's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1844 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c033.text: New map drawn after the 1850 census, which cut Maine's seats from 7 to 6. It was first used in the 1852 election.

c038.text: New map drawn after the 1860 census, which cut Maine's seats from 6 to 5. It was first used in the 1862 election.

c048.text: After the 1880 census changed Maine's seats from 5 to 4, Maine still elected all of its members statewide, so it had no districts to redraw.

c049.text: Maine's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1884 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c063.text: New map drawn after the 1910 census, which left Maine with 4 seats. It was first used in the 1912 election.

c073.text: New map drawn after the 1930 census, which cut Maine's seats from 4 to 3. It was first used in the 1932 election.

c088.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which cut Maine's seats from 3 to 2. It was first used in the 1962 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which left Maine with 2 seats. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left Maine with 2 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c104.text: Maine's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1994 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c109.text: New map following: State supreme court draws the map. When the legislature did not pass a congressional plan by the constitutional deadline, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court issued the districts itself on July 2, 2003.

c113.text: New map following: Desena v. Maine. Maine's schedule called for redrawing districts in 2013. A three-judge federal court ruled in June 2011 that the existing districts were unequal under the 2010 census and could not be used in 2012; the legislature passed a new map that September.

c115.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 2 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c118.text: New map following: Commission plan enacted after delay. Because census data arrived late, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court extended the redistricting deadlines in July 2021. The Apportionment Commission approved a congressional map on September 24, and the legislature enacted it on September 29, 2021.
